text:
B: Hi, can you hear me? I'm Klára, in London.
A: Yeah. Kacper. Swindon.
B: Hi. Erm, is Kacper a Polish name?
A: Yeah. I'm from Gdańsk. Came over when I was ten.
B: Oh, nice. I'm Czech, from Brno. So we are almost neighbours.
A: Sort of. Do you speak any Polish?
B: A little. I understand some, but I can't really speak it. There's a Polish shop near me on Hoe Street, I go there for the bread. Proper rye bread. But last week they ran out of the good one.
A: My mum makes her own. Sends tubs back with my sister. Pierogi, żurek.
B: Your mum makes żurek? Lucky. We have something similar. I make mostly soups, and svíčková for special days.
A: Don't know that one.
B: It's beef with a cream sauce and dumplings. It takes all day. My husband loves it. What do you do in Swindon?
A: Shift manager. Distribution centre, nights and weekends. Forty people.
B: Forty, that's a lot. Is it hard, managing people?
A: It's alright. Mostly it's people calling in sick. Someone always calls in sick on a Saturday.
B: (laughs) I worked in a shop on Oxford Street, it was the same. Always Saturday. Now I'm at home with my son, he's three and a half.
A: Right. Must be busy.
B: Yes. Today he woke me at half past five to tell me about a T. rex. So I'm a little tired.
A: I'm knackered too. Finished nights yesterday.
B: So we are both tired. Do you speak Polish at home?
A: With my mum, yeah. English everywhere else. I feel more Swindon, to be honest.
B: I understand. I speak Czech with my son, but he answers more and more in English. I worry he will lose it.
A: My sister worries about that too. If she has kids. She says she'll only speak Polish to them.
B: It's hard to do. You need to be stubborn.
A: Yeah. My mum was stubborn. That's probably why I still speak it.
B: Then she did a good job. Do you go back to Poland?
A: Once a year. Fly from Bristol. See my grandparents.
B: I go from Stansted. Always the early flight, with a toddler. Terrible.
A: Early flights are the worst. I'd rather drive.
B: To Gdańsk?
A: No. Probably not. Bit far.
